newsitem.title: FRANCE: France and Britain may extend Eurotunnel licence.
newsitem.headline: France and Britain may extend Eurotunnel licence.

text.p: The French finance ministry said on Tuesday the French and British governments were ready, on certain conditions, to extend Eurotunnel's licence to run the Channel Tunnel to at least 99 years,

Anglo-French firm Eurotunnel SA badly needed that extension, to woo dissident shareholders due to vote next week on a make-or-break deal to refinance 70 billion francs ($12 billion) of bank loans. The present licence runs for 65 years to 2052.
Executive chairman Patrick Ponsolle has said Eurotunnel faces bankrupcty if investors throw out the debt plan.

The news was the second big break for Eurotunnel in two days after Monday's announcement that a big U.S. investor had switched from opposing the restructuring and would vote for the refinancing deal at a July 10 meeting.
But Paris and London attached conditions to the lifeline.

The company must secure approval from the shareholders and 174 creditor banks on the debt plan and it must pay a share of profits to the governments from 2052, when the extension kicks in, and for the rest of the duration of the licence.
The governments also have to agree ways of boosting rail freight traffic through the tunnel, the finance ministry said in a statement.
Eurotunnel officials were not available for comment.

If the restructuring plan were rejected and if the creditor banks asked to exercise their rights under the "substitution clause," the governments would not be able to refuse them if the conditions stated in the concession were met, it said.
Under the terms of the substitution clause, the bankers can take control of the concession and change the management.
French minister for finance, economy and industry Dominique Strauss-Kahn welcomed the agreement on the licence extension, a separate statement from the minister said.

But before the extension can be implemented, negotiations between the governments and Eurotunnel have to be opened on the states' financial share from 2052 and on ways of increasing rail freight traffic through the Tunnel, it said.
"The extension of the concession opens significant opportunities for development for this great European project," it said. "This agreement is the states' contribution to Eurotunnel's problems."
Christian Cambier, chairman of the Eurotunnel Shareholders Association, a French group representing small investors, earlier said he would vote for the debt plan if the licence were extended.
"If there is no extension to the concession, I will vote 'no' he told Reuters, adding that if there were an extension, "I would vote yes."
Adacte, another smaller, more radical group of French investors, has said it would throw out the debt deal because there would still be significant financial risk even after the debt restructuring.

Eurotunnel said on Monday that U.S. fund Northern Cross Investments, which holds about three percent of the capital, has dropped its opposition to the refinancing and will back the management when the shareholders vote next week.

Shareholders have seen their investments plummet since the company came to the market in the late 1980s. The Tunnel opened late and over-budget due to building delays, suffered problems in servicing its debt and then a severe fire last November disrupted passenger and freight service.
Under the restructuring terms, banks will swap eight billion francs of loans for shares, but that will dilute the stockholders down to 54.5 percent of the equity capital. ($ = 5.883 French Francs)
